title: Introduction
text: Every computer language ever written is, at its core, a notation for describing computation. That idea — that computation itself could be formalized, written down, and reasoned about — did not begin with silicon. It began with mathematics. To understand why programming languages look the way they do, why they fight the battles they fight, and why the three languages in this notebook were chosen, you have to follow the thread back to where it starts.

title: Introduction
text: Every computer language ever written is, at its core, a notation for describing computation. That idea — that computation itself could be formalized, written down, and reasoned about — did not begin with silicon. It began with mathematics. To understand why programming languages look the way they do, why they fight the battles they fight, and why the three languages in this notebook were chosen, you have to follow the thread back to where it starts.

title: Introduction
text:
The Mathematical Roots

Leibniz and the Dream of a Universal Calculus
In the late 17th century, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz dreamed of a calculus ratiocinator — a universal calculating system that could reduce all reasoning to symbol manipulation. If arguments could be encoded as symbols and symbols manipulated by rule, then disputes between scholars could be resolved not by debate but by calculation: “Let us compute.” The dream was centuries ahead of its time. Leibniz did not achieve it. But he invented the binary number system and built mechanical calculators, and the dream itself proved contagious.


Boole and the Algebra of Thought
In 1854, George Boole published An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, establishing that logical propositions — AND, OR, NOT — could be treated as algebraic expressions. True and false became 1 and 0. Inference became arithmetic. This was not yet computing, but it was the algebra that would eventually run inside every transistor on every chip ever made. Boolean logic is the bedrock below the bedrock.


Babbage and Lovelace

The First Programmers

Charles Babbage spent decades designing mechanical computing engines. His Difference Engine (1822) could tabulate polynomial functions. His Analytical Engine (1837) was far more ambitious: it had a store (memory), a mill (processor), and it could be directed by punched cards. It was never built in his lifetime, but the design was sound.
Ada Lovelace, working from Babbage’s notes, wrote what is now recognized as the first computer program: an algorithm for computing Bernoulli numbers on the Analytical Engine. More importantly, she saw what Babbage himself underestimated — that a machine that could manipulate symbols by rule was not merely a calculator. It was a general-purpose engine for transforming any information that could be encoded. She wrote in 1843:

“The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.”

That sentence contains both the power and the humility of every programming language ever written. The machine does exactly what you tell it. The craft is knowing how to tell it correctly.

title: Introduction
text:
The Theoretical Foundations

Church and the Lambda Calculus
In the 1930s, Alonzo Church developed the lambda calculus — a formal system for expressing computation using function abstraction and application. On paper, with Greek letters, he showed that any computable function could be expressed as the application of anonymous functions to arguments. Lambda calculus has no loops, no variables in the imperative sense, no state. Just functions calling functions.
This sounds abstract, but it is the direct ancestor of functional programming. Every time you write an anonymous function — a lambda, a closure, an arrow function — you are using Church’s notation, imported wholesale into modern languages.


Turing and the Machine
In 1936, Alan Turing published “On Computable Numbers,” introducing the Turing machine: an abstract device with an infinite tape, a read/write head, and a finite set of rules. Given the right rules, it could simulate any mechanical process. Turing proved that certain problems were undecidable — no algorithm could solve them — and in doing so, he defined the boundary of what computation can and cannot do.
Church and Turing arrived at the same boundary from opposite directions. The Church-Turing thesis holds that any effectively computable function is computable by a Turing machine and expressible in the lambda calculus. This equivalence — between the procedural model (do this, then that, change this register) and the functional model (apply this function to that value) — echoes through the history of programming languages as a recurring argument about which style is more natural, more correct, more powerful.


Von Neumann and the Stored-Program Architecture
The theoretical work of Church and Turing became physical in the 1940s. John von Neumann’s 1945 report on the EDVAC computer articulated what became the dominant architecture of the modern computer: a processor and a memory that holds both data and instructions. Programs are not external configurations wired into the machine; they are data stored in the same space as the numbers they compute on.
This insight — the stored-program computer — is why programming is possible at all. A program is data. You can write programs that read programs. You can write compilers. You can write operating systems. The entire software stack rests on this one architectural decision.

title: Introduction
text:
The Generations of Language
With the theoretical groundwork laid and machines finally built, the question became practical: how do humans tell the machine what to do? The answer evolved through recognizable generations.

First Generation

Machine Code (1940s)

The earliest computers were programmed in machine code — raw binary instructions specific to the processor’s hardware. A programmer working on the ENIAC in 1945 set switches, plugged cables, and read reference cards mapping decimal operation codes to physical behaviors. There was no abstraction. Every instruction was a direct hardware command.



Era
Representation
Example




Machine Code
Binary / Hex opcodes
B8 01 00 00 00


Assembly
Mnemonic + operands
MOV EAX, 1


High-Level
Language statement
int x = 1;



Machine code is still what runs on every processor today. Every other generation is a translation layer.


Second Generation

Assembly Language (1950s)

Assembly language replaced raw opcodes with human-readable mnemonics. MOV, ADD, JMP. An assembler — itself a program — translates these mnemonics one-for-one into machine code. One mnemonic becomes one instruction. The 1:1 relationship is the defining characteristic of assembly. There is no abstraction about what the processor will do; you are telling it exactly which registers to move, which memory addresses to read.
Assembly gave programmers legibility without sacrificing control. It remains the language of choice anywhere the hardware itself must be negotiated directly: bootloaders, interrupt handlers, cycle-critical DSP routines, embedded microcontrollers with 256 bytes of RAM. It is covered in this notebook for exactly that reason.


Third Generation

High-Level Languages (1950s–1970s)

Third-generation languages introduced abstraction — one statement expanding into many machine instructions. A for loop, a function call, a variable — these have no direct equivalent in hardware. The compiler invents the translation.
The major milestones:








Year
Language
Significance




1957
FORTRAN
First compiled high-level language. Proved that compilers could match hand-tuned assembly in performance. Scientific computing.


1958
LISP
First functional language. Lists and lambda abstraction. Influenced nearly every dynamic language since.


1959
COBOL
Business data processing. English-like syntax. Ran the world’s financial infrastructure for decades (and still does).


1960
ALGOL 60
Introduced block structure, lexical scoping, and the grammar that most modern languages still use. Never widely deployed but enormously influential.


1964
BASIC
Designed to be simple enough that non-specialists could program. Brought computing to universities and, eventually, homes.


1972
C
Systems programming. Close enough to the machine to write operating systems, fast enough to replace assembly in most contexts. The lingua franca of computing.


1975
Scheme
Minimal, elegant Lisp dialect. Lexical scope, tail recursion, first-class continuations. A language for teaching the nature of computation.

title: Introduction
text:
The Great Schisms

The Structured Programming Revolution
In the 1960s, programs grew large enough to become unmanageable. The culprit, according to Edsger Dijkstra’s 1968 letter “Go To Statement Considered Harmful,” was the GOTO — the unconditional jump that let control flow anywhere in the program. Large programs with many GOTOs became impossible to reason about. Dijkstra argued that control flow should be structured: sequences, conditionals, and loops only.
Structured programming — the discipline of using if, while, and for instead of GOTO — is now so universal it is invisible. Every language in this notebook is a structured language. But the fight was real, and the resolution shaped what “good code” means to this day.


Object-Oriented Programming
In 1967, Simula introduced the concepts of objects and classes — bundles of data and behavior that could model real-world entities. Smalltalk, developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, refined the idea into a pure philosophy: everything is an object; computation is objects sending messages to each other.
C++ brought object-oriented programming to the systems world in 1983, adding classes to C without abandoning its performance characteristics. Java (1995) brought it to the masses with a garbage-collected, platform-independent runtime. By the 1990s, OOP had won the mainstream. Almost every language taught in universities was object-oriented.
OOP solved real problems. It gave large teams a vocabulary for decomposing complex systems. But it also introduced its own complexity: deep inheritance hierarchies, mutable shared state, a tendency toward architecture for architecture’s sake. The reaction against OOP’s excesses would shape the next generation of systems languages.


The Functional Renaissance
Lisp had been functional since 1958, but functional programming remained academic for decades. In the 1980s and 1990s, ML and Haskell developed rigorous type systems built around functional ideas: immutability, algebraic data types, pattern matching, monads. These were not primarily practical languages; they were laboratories for type theory.
The ideas escaped the laboratory. Erlang (1986) used functional techniques to build massively concurrent, fault-tolerant telephone infrastructure. Scala (2004) fused functional and object-oriented programming on the JVM. Clojure (2007) brought a Lisp to the JVM with a pragmatic emphasis on immutability and concurrency. And mainstream languages — Java, C#, Python, JavaScript — absorbed functional features one by one: lambdas, map/filter/reduce, pattern matching, immutable data structures.
The insight that functional programming gave the world was this: mutable shared state is the root of most concurrency bugs. If data cannot change, threads cannot corrupt each other. This insight became urgent as multi-core processors became standard, and it drove a resurgence of interest in functional design throughout the 2000s and 2010s.

title: Introduction
text:
The Safety Problem
As software grew to run aircraft, medical devices, financial systems, and critical infrastructure, the cost of bugs became existential. And one category of bug proved devastatingly common: memory errors.
C and C++ give programmers direct control over memory. That control enables extraordinary performance and hardware access. It also enables buffer overflows, use-after-free errors, null pointer dereferences, and data races — entire classes of vulnerabilities that have caused some of the most catastrophic security failures in computing history. The Morris Worm (1988), Heartbleed (2014), and countless others traced to memory mismanagement in C and C++ code.
For decades, the response was tooling: valgrind, AddressSanitizer, static analyzers, fuzzing. The tools helped. But they were detective, not preventive.
The alternative — garbage-collected languages like Java, Python, Go — solve memory safety by taking memory management away from the programmer entirely. The garbage collector tracks allocations and frees them when no references remain. This works remarkably well. But it comes with a cost: unpredictable pause times, higher memory overhead, and an inability to reason precisely about when and where resources are released. For systems programming — operating systems, device drivers, real-time signal processing — these costs are often unacceptable.

title: Introduction
text:
The Modern Era

Rust and the Safety-Performance Synthesis

For most of computing history, you chose between safety and control. Garbage-collected languages gave you safety at the cost of performance and predictability. C and C++ gave you control at the cost of safety. The assumption was that this tradeoff was fundamental.
Rust (1.0 released 2015) challenged that assumption directly. Its core innovation is the ownership system: a set of compile-time rules enforced by the type checker that guarantee memory safety and thread safety without a garbage collector. Every value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is freed — automatically, deterministically, at compile time. Borrowing rules prevent data races. The borrow checker rejects programs that would cause undefined behavior before they ever run.
The result is a language with:

No garbage collector — deterministic performance, suitable for real-time systems
No runtime — small binary size, suitable for embedded targets
Memory safety — no buffer overflows, no use-after-free, no null pointer dereferences, guaranteed by the compiler
Thread safety — data races are compile errors, not runtime crashes
C-compatible FFI — can call into C libraries and be called from C

Rust did not appear from nowhere. It synthesized decades of research: region-based memory management from ML, affine type systems from linear logic, ownership semantics from earlier systems research. But it was the first language to package these ideas into a practical, production-ready systems language with a coherent community and toolchain.
The response from industry was unusual for a new systems language: enthusiastic adoption. Mozilla used Rust to rewrite performance-critical parts of Firefox. Microsoft began rewriting Windows components in Rust. The Linux kernel accepted Rust as a second implementation language in 2022. The U.S. National Security Agency and CISA issued guidance recommending Rust and other memory-safe languages for new systems development. The narrative that safety and systems performance were irreconcilable was broken.

title: Introduction
text:
Why These Three Languages
This notebook covers Assembly, C, and Rust. The choice is not arbitrary — it follows the spine of systems programming evolution:
Machine Code → Assembly → C → Rust
Each step adds abstraction while preserving the core concern: control over what the machine actually does.
Assembly is the floor. It is what the processor executes. Understanding assembly means understanding what a for loop actually is (a branch and a counter), what a function call actually costs (a stack frame), and why cache misses matter (a load instruction that stalls for 200 cycles). Every higher-level language compiles to this, and knowing it makes you a better programmer in every language above it.
C is the lingua franca. It is the language in which operating systems, compilers, databases, and embedded firmware are written. It is what assembly became when programmers needed to write programs larger than a single human could hold in mind. Understanding C means understanding pointers, stack and heap allocation, the cost of indirection, and why undefined behavior is the way it is. C is also the interface language of the world — the FFI that every other language speaks when it needs to talk to hardware or to existing systems.
Rust is the synthesis. It carries C’s performance and control into an era that demands safety guarantees C cannot provide. It is the answer to the question: what would C look like if it were designed today, with everything we have learned in fifty years about type theory, memory safety, and concurrent programming? Rust is not a replacement for C in the sense of being able to run everywhere C runs — not yet — but it is a demonstration that the tradeoffs C was built around are not immutable laws.
Together, these three languages span from the metal to the modern, from direct hardware manipulation to compile-time safety proofs. Understanding all three means understanding not just how to write programs, but why programs are the shape they are — why the machine works as it does, why the language constrains you where it does, and what the tradeoffs cost.
That is what this notebook is about.

title: Introduction
section: A Note on What Gets Left Out
text:
A Note on What Gets Left Out
The history above covers the threads most relevant to systems programming. It omits or mentions only in passing:

SQL and declarative languages — a wholly different paradigm where you describe what you want, not how to compute it
Prolog and logic programming — computation as proof search
Scripting languages — Python, Ruby, Perl, JavaScript — which prioritized developer productivity and dynamic typing over static guarantees
Domain-specific languages — from TeX to VHDL to MATLAB — built for one purpose with the rest left out

These are not lesser paths. They reflect different answers to the same question: what does a useful notation for computation look like? The answer depends entirely on what you need to compute, and for whom.
The languages in this notebook are the ones you need if the machine itself is part of what you are programming. If you need to be close to the hardware — close enough that you care about register allocation, stack depth, cache behavior, and memory layout — this is your lineage.
The next chapter begins where computation itself begins: assembly language and the direct instruction of hardware.

text:
The name “Git” was coined by its creator, Linus Torvalds, “I’m an egotistical bastard, and I name all my projects after myself. First ‘Linux’, now ‘git’”. In British English slang, a “git” is an unpleasant, silly, or incompetent person.

title: Git Reference Manual
section: The Anatomy of a Git Repository
text:
The Anatomy of a Git Repository

The Three Trees and the Object Database

To understand how Git tracks changes, you must look past your visible project files. Git manages your project using three internal conceptual areas (often called the Three Trees) backed by a simple key-value object database inside the hidden .git folder.

The Three Trees





Efficient Git usage relies on knowing which “tree” you are currently manipulating.

The Working Directory (The Sandbox): This is the actual file system on your computer where you modify files. These files are real, physical assets you open in your IDE.
The Staging Area / Index (The Blueprint): A single, binary file located at .git/index. It acts as a preparation area that calculates exactly what the next snapshot will look like. When you run git add, you are taking a snapshot of your files at that exact moment and staging them.
The Commit History / HEAD (The Vault): This is the permanent record. When you run git commit, Git takes the blueprint from the Staging Area and permanently writes it into the local database as a commit object. HEAD is simply a pointer showing which commit in the vault your Working Directory is currently reflecting.










Action
Source Tree
Target Tree
Command




Stage Changes
Working Directory
Staging Area
git add <file>


Commit Changes
Staging Area
Local Repository
git commit


Unstage Changes
Local Repository / HEAD
Staging Area
git reset <file>


Discard Local Changes
Staging Area
Working Directory
git checkout -- <file>





The Content-Addressable Storage

The .git/objects Directory

Git does not track file deltas (the differences between version A and version B). Instead, it acts as a content-addressable key-value store. When you stage or commit a file, Git compresses the content, hashes it using a cryptographic algorithm (SHA-1 or SHA-256), and stores it in .git/objects.
The resulting 40-character hexadecimal string acts as both the unique identifier and the exact folder path to that data. If the content of a file does not change, its hash does not change, meaning Git only stores a single copy of that file across your entire history, no matter how many commits reference it.
Inside .git/objects, Git breaks data down into four primary object types:
.git/objects/
├── [First 2 chars of hash]/
│   └── [Remaining 38 chars of hash]  --> (A zipped Blob, Tree, or Commit)

1. Blobs

Binary Large Objects

A blob stores raw file data. It contains only the text or data of a file, completely stripped of metadata. A blob does not know its own filename, its folder structure, or its modification date. It only knows its content.


2. Trees
A tree object solves the mystery of the missing filenames. A tree represents a directory. It is a simple text manifest that maps the SHA-1 hashes of blobs back to their actual filenames, permissions, and directory locations. Trees can also point to other trees to represent nested subdirectories.


3. Commits
A commit object is a small text file pointing to a specific top-level tree object (the snapshot of the project root at that moment). It contains metadata: the author, the committer, the timestamp, the commit log message, and a pointer to one or more parent commits (the hashes of the commits that came immediately before it). This chain of parent pointers forms your history graph.


4. Annotated Tags
A tag is an explicit, unchanging pointer containing a commit hash, a tagger name, a message, and a timestamp, used to flag release points like v1.0.0.



Putting It All Together

The Commit Mechanism

When you make a single commit changing one file in a subfolder:

Git writes a new blob for the modified file content.
Git writes a new tree for the subfolder to map the new blob to its filename.
Git writes a new top-level tree for the repository root to link to the updated subfolder tree. Unchanged folders continue to point to their existing, older tree objects.
Git writes a commit object pointing to the new root tree and listing the previous commit hash as its parent.
Git updates your current branch pointer (which is just a text file inside .git/refs/heads/) to point to the hash of this new commit object.

title: Git Reference Manual
text:
Search & Investigation
Investigation in Git falls into two fundamentally different activities, and confusing them is the source of most frustration. The first is searching a single snapshot: “where, in the code as it exists right now, does this function live?” The second is searching across history: “when, across the thousands of snapshots in my object database, did this line appear, change, or vanish?” The working tree is a single point in time; history is the entire DAG of commits behind it. Different questions, different tools. The subsections below are ordered from the gentlest (walking the timeline) to the most surgical (binary-searching the graph for a regression).

Basic Navigation & History

Exploring the Timeline

Everything here is built on a single command, git log, which is simply a walk over the parent pointers introduced earlier. Recall that each commit object stores a hash of its parent (Commits); git log starts at HEAD and follows those pointers backwards, printing each commit it visits. That is the entire mechanism. Every flag below is just a filter applied to that walk: --author discards commits whose author field doesn’t match, --since discards commits outside a time window, and -- <file_path> discards commits whose snapshot didn’t touch that path. Because it is a graph walk and not a flat list, --graph can draw the branch and merge topology directly, and --all tells the walk to start from every branch tip rather than just your current HEAD.








Objective
Command
Purpose / Context




Visual History
git log --oneline --graph --all
Displays a compact, visual representation of all branches, merges, and commits.


Filter by Author
git log --author="Name"
Restricts the history to commits made by a specific person.


Filter by Date
git log --since="2 weeks ago"
Restricts the history to a specific timeframe (e.g., --since, --until).


Filter by File
git log -- <file_path>
Shows only the commits that modified a specific file or directory.


Search Commit Messages
git log --grep="fix memory leak"
Filters the walk to commits whose log message matches the pattern.


Inspect a Commit
git show <hash>
Displays the log message and full diff of exactly what changed in that commit.









Note



--grep searches the commit message, the human prose you wrote. This is a different axis entirely from -S and -G in the Advanced Code Tracing table below, which search the content of the diff (the code itself). “Find the commit where someone mentioned the leak” versus “find the commit where the leaking line actually changed” are distinct questions, and Git gives you a distinct flag for each.




Searching the Working Tree

git grep vs. the System grep

This is the “single snapshot” half of investigation, and it is worth being explicit about why a dedicated tool exists. You could run the ordinary system grep -r over your project folder, but it has no idea what Git is tracking: it will descend into node_modules, dredge up build artifacts, and search files you have told Git to ignore. git grep searches only the contents Git knows about, which makes it both faster (it consults the index rather than stat-ing every file on disk) and cleaner (it honors .gitignore). Critically, it can also search any past snapshot without touching your working directory: by naming a commit or tag, you ask Git to decompress that historical tree and search it in place, then hand you the results while your checked-out files stay exactly as they are.








Objective
Command
Purpose / Context




Search Current Code
git grep "pattern"
Searches all tracked files in the working tree; respects .gitignore.


Show Line Numbers
git grep -n "pattern"
Prepends the line number to each match for direct navigation.


Search a Past Snapshot
git grep "pattern" <commit_or_tag>
Searches the content of any historical commit or tag without checking it out.


Count Matches per File
git grep -c "pattern"
Reports how many times the pattern appears in each file rather than the lines themselves.





Working with Tags

Locating and Understanding Releases

It is worth clearing up exactly where tags live, because it explains why their search commands behave the way they do. A tag is not part of any branch. Branches and tags are both just refs, named pointers to a commit hash, but they sit in different drawers: branches in .git/refs/heads/, tags in .git/refs/tags/. The difference is behavioral. A branch ref moves forward automatically every time you commit on it; a tag ref never moves on its own once created. So a tag isn’t anchored to a branch at all, it is anchored directly to a single commit. That commit may happen to be reachable from several branches, or from none (if every branch that once contained it has since moved on), and the tag will sit there pointing at it regardless.
This is why git tag lists every tag in the repository rather than “the tags on this branch”, the concept of “tags on a branch” doesn’t exist. When you genuinely want the branch relationship, you have to ask the inverse question with git branch --contains: given this tagged commit, which branches have it somewhere in their ancestry?








Objective
Command
Purpose / Context




List All Tags
git tag
Outputs a list of all tags in the repository (tags are global, not per-branch).


Search Tags by Pattern
git tag -l "v2.0*"
Filters the tag list using wildcard patterns to find specific versions.


Inspect a Tag
git show <tag_name>
Displays the tag’s metadata (annotated message, tagger) and the commit it points to.


Find Branches with Tag
git branch --contains <tag_name>
Lists all branches that have this tag’s commit in their ancestry line.





Advanced Code Tracing

Git as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)

This is the “across history” half of investigation, and it leans entirely on the structure built in The Anatomy of a Git Repository. Because Git stores full snapshots linked by parent pointers (Commits) rather than a flat changelog, you are not searching a list, you are traversing a Directed Acyclic Graph: directed because parent pointers run one way (backwards in time), acyclic because a commit can never be its own ancestor. The tools below query that graph by content transformation. Rather than asking “what is in this commit”, they ask “between a commit and its parent, did this string’s count change, did this regex appear in the diff, did this specific line get rewritten?” That comparison against the parent is what lets you pinpoint the exact moment a piece of code came into being.
The two pickaxe variants are easy to confuse, so the distinction is worth stating plainly. -S is a counting search: it flags a commit only when the number of occurrences of your string differs from the parent, which answers “where was this added or removed?” -G is a content search: it flags any commit whose diff has an added or removed line matching your regex, even if the total count is unchanged, which answers “where was a line containing this touched at all?” Reach for -S to find an introduction or deletion; reach for -G to catch a modification that -S would miss because the line was edited rather than added.








Objective
Command
Purpose / Context




Find String Addition/Removal
git log -S "search_string" --oneline
Locates commits where the absolute count of the string changed. (The “Pickaxe” search).


Find String Regular Expression
git log -G "regex_pattern" -p
Locates commits where an added or removed diff line matches the pattern, even if the count is unchanged.


Track Line History Range
git log -L <start>,<end>:<file_path>
Traces the evolution of specific line ranges across time.


Trace File Rename History
git log --follow -- <file_path>
Ensures history tracking persists across file renames.


Inspect Line Ancestry
git blame -w -M <file_path>
Displays author and commit hash for each line, ignoring whitespace (-w) and moving lines within the file (-M).


Blame Past a Noise Commit
git blame <commit>^ -- <file_path>
Re-runs blame against the parent of a known formatting commit, skipping it to reveal the real author beneath.





Hunting a Regression

git bisect

The tools above find where code lives; git bisect finds which commit broke something, and it is the most powerful investigation tool Git offers. The insight is that your history is a sorted sequence: somewhere along the chain of commits there is a transition from “working” to “broken”, and you want the single commit where that flip happened. Checking every commit one by one is linear, but because the commits are ordered, you can binary-search them instead. Tell Git one commit that is known good and one that is known bad, and it checks out the commit halfway between them. You test it and report good or bad; Git discards the half that cannot contain the transition and bisects again. A history of a thousand commits collapses to roughly ten tests.








Objective
Command
Purpose / Context




Begin a Hunt
git bisect start
Enters bisect mode, ready to receive the boundary commits.


Mark the Boundaries
git bisect bad  git bisect good <hash>
Declares the current commit broken and an older commit known to work.


Report a Test Result
git bisect good / git bisect bad
Reports the checked-out midpoint, prompting Git to narrow the range further.


Automate the Search
git bisect run <test_command>
Runs a script at each step, using its exit code to mark commits automatically.


End the Hunt
git bisect reset
Restores HEAD to where you started before the bisect began.





Recovering Lost Work

git reflog

Not all investigation is about other people’s code; sometimes you need to investigate your own recent past, usually after a rebase or reset that seems to have eaten your commits. Here is the reassuring truth: those commits are almost never gone. When a branch ref moves off a commit, the commit object still sits in the database; it has merely become unreachable, with no ref pointing at it. The reflog is Git’s private journal of everywhere HEAD and your branch tips have pointed, recorded every time they moved. It is purely local and never pushed. Because it remembers the hash a ref held before your destructive command, it gives you the address of the “lost” commit so you can point a branch back at it and bring it back to life.








Objective
Command
Purpose / Context




View HEAD Movements
git reflog
Lists recent positions of HEAD with their hashes and the action that moved them.


Inspect a Lost Commit
git show HEAD@{2}
Shows the commit HEAD pointed to two moves ago, using reflog’s positional syntax.


Recover to a Prior State
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
Moves your branch back to where it was one action ago, undoing a bad reset or rebase.


Rescue an Orphaned Commit
git branch rescue <lost_hash>
Anchors a new branch to a commit found in the reflog, making it reachable again.





Tutorial

Tracking the Origins of Code

When a standard git blame shows a generic “Refactor formatting” commit instead of the actual author of the logic, the file’s ancestry must be traced backwards.

Locate the line range of interest in your file (e.g., lines 45 through 60 in analysis.qmd).
Execute the line-log search to filter the DAG down to only modifications affecting those lines: bash     git log -L 45,60:analysis.qmd --oneline
Identify the root commit at the bottom of this generated log.
If the code was introduced from another file entirely, run a pickaxe search using a signature keyword or definition from that snippet across the whole history: bash     git log -S "void calculate_weights" -p --raw

If git blame keeps stopping at the same formatting commit, blame its parent instead to step past the noise and find the commit that actually wrote the logic:
git blame <formatting_commit>^ -- analysis.qmd

title: Git Reference Manual
text:
Managing Diverged Branches

merge vs. rebase


The Concept

Divergence Architecture

Branches diverge when your local branch and its remote counterpart (or a base branch like main) both receive unique commits after their last common ancestor.
          B---C [feature] (Your Local Branch)
         /
    A---D---E [main] (Remote / Shared Branch)
To integrate changes from main into feature, you have two structural options:

Explicit Merge (git merge): Creates a non-destructive, multi-parent merge commit (F). Preserves historical reality but introduces non-linear topology (“train tracks”).
Rebase (git rebase): Rewrites history by moving the entire sequence of your local commits (B, C) to the tip of the target branch (E). This creates new commits (B', C') with identical content but new hashes, yielding a perfectly linear history.

                B'---C' [feature] (Rewritten History)
               /
    A---D---E [main]


Reference & Commands








Objective
Command
Structural Impact




Standard Merge
git merge main
Creates a merge commit; preserves chronological branch context.


Linear Rebase
git rebase main
Replays local commits sequentially on top of target branch base.


Abort Operations
git merge --abort  git rebase --abort
Halts execution and restores the index and working tree to pre-operation states.


Conflict Discovery
git status
Lists unmerged paths requiring manual intervention.





Tutorial

Resolving Divergence with Minimal Friction

When your local branch cannot be pushed because the remote tracking branch has new work, use a rebase-driven alignment to avoid creating unnecessary merge loops.

Fetch current upstream state without shifting your HEAD pointer: bash     git fetch origin
Initiate the rebase on top of the updated remote branch (e.g., main): bash     git rebase origin/main
Handle Conflicts Immediatley: If Git pauses due to conflicting edits, it will leave the markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) directly in your source files.

Open the affected file.
The top block (between HEAD and =======) represents the upstream state from main.
The bottom block (between ======= and your commit hash) represents your local changes.
Edit the file to unify the logic, removing all conflict markers.

Stage and Progress: Do not run a new commit command. Stage the resolved assets and instruct the rebase engine to proceed to your next commit: bash     git add path/to/resolved_file.qmd     git rebase --continue

title: Git Reference Manual
text:
Interactive Rebasing

rebase -i


The Concept

History Sanitization

Interactive rebasing provides precise control over local commits before sharing them with an upstream repository. It allows you to clean up erratic commit history (“fixed typo”, “trying again”, “actual fix”) into clean, logical semantic units.

Absolute Rule: Never interactively rebase commits that have already been pushed to a public or shared repository. Rewriting shared history invalidates the commit hashes of your collaborators, breaking their downstream trees.



Reference & Commands








Sub-Command / Action
Syntax in Instruction Sheet
Functional Mechanics




pick
pick <hash> <message>
Retains the commit exactly as it is.


reword
reword <hash> <message>
Retains the commit content but opens an editor to rewrite the log message.


edit
edit <hash> <message>
Halts execution at this commit to allow modification of file contents.


squash
squash <hash> <message>
Melds the commit content into the previous commit, combining log messages.


fixup
fixup <hash> <message>
Melds the commit content into the previous commit, discarding this commit’s log message.


drop
drop <hash> <message>
Removes the commit entirely from the branch history.





Tutorial

Cleaning Up Your Local Commits

Assume you have made 4 commits locally, but the middle two are intermediate fixes that clutter the project log.

Launch the interactive editor targetting the last 4 commits on your current branch: bash     git rebase -i HEAD~4
Analyze the instruction list: An editor window will open showing your commits chronologically from top to bottom (the reverse of git log). text     pick a1b2c3d Initial data ingestion script     pick e5f6g7h Fix broken file path handling     pick i9j0k1l Typo correction in headers     pick m3n4o5p Complete visualization pipeline
Modify the operations: Change the instructions to consolidate the intermediate commits into the primary ingestion script. text     pick a1b2c3d Initial data ingestion script     fixup e5f6g7h Fix broken file path handling     fixup i9j0k1l Typo correction in headers     pick m3n4o5p Complete visualization pipeline
Save and Close the editor. Git will sequentially apply a1b2c3d, merge the structural changes of the next two commits directly into it without changing its intent, and then apply m3n4o5p. Your history is now condensed into two pristine commits.

title: Git Reference Manual
text:
Git Submodules

The Concept

Pointers to External Repositories

A Git submodule is a fully independent Git repository embedded within a subdirectory of a parent (“superproject”) repository. Crucially, the parent repository does not track the file contents of the submodule. Instead, it tracks exactly two things:

The submodule path and its source URL (recorded in a .gitmodules file).
A gitlink entry: a specific, fixed commit hash pointing to the exact state of the submodule repository.



Reference & Commands








Objective
Command
Scope




Clone Parent with Submodules
git clone --recurse-submodules <url>
Clones the superproject and automatically checks out all internal submodules.


Initialize Existing Submodules
git submodule update --init --recursive
Configures and fetches data for submodules if cloned without the recursive flag.


Check Submodule Status
git submodule status
Displays current active hashes of submodules; a leading - indicates uninitialized state.


Pull Submodule Changes
git submodule update --remote --merge
Fetches the newest modifications from the remote tracking branch specified in .gitmodules.





Tutorial

Resolving Out-of-Sync Submodules

A common point of failure occurs when a collaborator updates a submodule reference on a remote branch, and your local workspace falls out of sync after a pull, resulting in modified dirty working directories.

Pull the latest parent commits: bash     git pull origin main
Running git status may show the submodule directory as modified or untracked because your local pointer has moved in history, but the physical files in that directory haven’t shifted yet.
Synchronize the physical files to match the precise commit hash expected by the parent project: bash     git submodule update --init --recursive
Making edits inside a submodule: If you need to make changes to the submodule library itself:

Change into the submodule directory: cd path/to/submodule.
Check out an active branch (submodules default to a “detached HEAD” state): git checkout main.
Stage, commit, and push your changes within the submodule repository first.
Return to the parent repository (cd ..) and commit the new submodule pointer change so the superproject links to your new work.

title: Git Reference Manual
text:
Emergency Recovery Options

The Concept

The Safety Net (git reflog)

Git almost never deletes anything that has been committed. Even when you rewrite history, delete a branch, or perform a destructive rebase, the old commits remain dangling in your database for a grace period (typically 30–90 days). The Reference Log (reflog) records every single movement of the HEAD pointer on your local machine.


Reference & Commands








Objective
Command
Context




View Local Pointer History
git reflog
Chronological list of every action that shifted your local HEAD pointer.


Restore a Specific State
git reset --hard HEAD@{index}
Destructively forces working directory, staging area, and branch pointer to a specific reflog state.


Undo Last Local Commit
git reset --soft HEAD~1
Uncommits the last change, preserving your modifications safely in your staging area.


Wipe Untracked Files
git clean -fd
Forcefully removes untracked files (-f) and directories (-d) from the workspace.





Tutorial

Recovering from a Destructive Rebase

If you run a rebase that goes completely wrong, corrupts your code, or deletes crucial commits, you can use the reflog to time-travel back to the moment before the rebase started.

Query the local reference log: bash     git reflog
Analyze the output log from top to bottom (most recent actions are at the top): text     7a8b9c0 HEAD@{0}: rebase (continue): Finished rebase onto origin/main     3d4e5f6 HEAD@{1}: rebase (step): Applied commit "Fixed typo"     1a2b3c4 HEAD@{2}: rebase (start): checkout origin/main     987f65e HEAD@{3}: commit: Ready for production architecture
Locate the entry right before the rebase mechanics began. In this case, HEAD@{3} represents your pristine local state before the rebase started.
Hard-reset your branch back to that safe coordinate: bash     git reset --hard HEAD@{3}

Your working directory and commit history are now restored exactly as they existed before the operation.

title: The C Language
text:
C is a general-purpose, procedural computer programming language supporting structured programming, lexical variable scope, and recursion. It provides constructs that map efficiently to typical machine instructions, making it the “lingua franca” of embedded systems and Digital Signal Processing (DSP). It sits at the intersection of high-level readability and low-level hardware control.





The original ANSI C standard defined 32 keywords. These are reserved words that cannot be used as variable names. They form the skeleton of the language:









Data Types

unsigned









C provides a rich Standard Library (often referred to as libc). Unlike higher-level languages, C does not have built-in statements for Input/Output (I/O). Instead, I/O is handled by functions in the standard library, primarily defined in <stdio.h>.

printf / scanf: The workhorses for formatted output and input.
fprintf / fscanf: Versions that work with file streams.







NoteWhat is stdout on Embedded Systems?



In an embedded context (like the dsPIC): There is no “screen” or “keyboard” by default. The standard library functions must be “retargeted.” This usually means the low-level functions that printf calls (often named write or _mon_putc) are implemented by the developer to send characters byte-by-byte over a peripheral like UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter). Thus, printf("Hello") effectively sends 5 bytes out of the serial port to your computer’s terminal.





A compiler is a program that translates computer code written in one programming language (the source language, like C) into another language (the target language, usually machine code or assembly). For the dsPIC, we typically use the XC16 compiler.



A linker is a utility program that takes one or more object files generated by a compiler and combines them into a single executable file, library file, or another ‘object’ file. It resolves references between different modules (e.g., if main.c calls a function defined in dsp.c).

title: The C Language
The C Language
The C Language
text:
The Build
The “build” is the process of converting your entire project (source files, headers, configuration
bits) into a machine-readable format.
In an embedded context, this output is often a HEX file. This file is not run by an OS like an .exe on Windows; instead, it is “flashed” directly into the microcontroller’s non-volatile program memory.
The build process also generates a Map File, which is critical for debugging. It shows exactly where every function and variable is placed in the device’s memory.

title: The C Language
The C Language
text:
Optimization
Optimization allows the compiler to adjust the code to improve performance or reduce size, often at the expense of compilation time and debuggability.

Compiler Optimization Levels

-O0: No optimization. Best for debugging as code flow matches source lines exactly.
-O1: Moderate optimization.
-O2: High optimization for speed.
-Os: Optimize for size (crucial when flash memory is limited).



The volatile Keyword
In embedded C, volatile is perhaps the most important qualifier. It tells the compiler: “The value of this variable may change at any time, without any action being taken by the code the compiler finds nearby.”
This prevents the compiler from optimizing away reads/writes to:

Hardware Registers: A status flag might change due to an interrupt, not software flow.
Global Variables: Shared between an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) and the main loop.

// Without volatile, the compiler might replace this loop with a generic 'while(true)'
// or remove the read entirely if it thinks the value never changes.
volatile int *status_reg = 0xFF00;
while (*status_reg == 0); // Wait for hardware flag

title: The C Language
text:
Features and Libraries for DSP
Digital Signal Processing requires specific features to handle continuous signals efficiently.

Fixed-Point Arithmetic
While floating-point is easy to use, many DSCs (Digital Signal Controllers) are optimized for fixed-point arithmetic. This represents fractional numbers using integers, trading dynamic range for speed and determinism.

Fractional Representation

1.15 Format







NoteQ15



Q15 (or 1.15) is a fixed-point number format where:

1 bit is used for the sign.
15 bits are used for the fractional part. This allows representing numbers in the range \([-1, 0.999969]\). It is widely used in 16-bit DSPs because it maps perfectly to the 16-bit integer registers.



In 16-bit DSPs, we often use the Q15 (or 1.15) format.

The 16 bits are treated as a signed integer range \([-32768, +32767]\).
Conceptually, we divide this integer by \(2^{15}\) (32768).
Range: \(-1.0\) to \(\approx 0.999969\).
0x7FFF (32767) represents \(\approx 1.0\).
0x8000 (-32768) represents \(-1.0\).

Arithmetic: When you multiply two Q15 numbers, the result is conceptually Q30 (since \(2^{-15} \times 2^{-15} = 2^{-30}\)). To store this back into a 16-bit Q15 variable, you must shift the result to the right by 15 bits.
\[
Result_{Q15} = (A_{Q15} \times B_{Q15}) >> 15
\]
DSP hardware often does this shift (and handles saturation so overflows don’t wrap around to negative numbers) automatically in a single cycle.



DSP Extensions and Intrinsics
Standard C does not natively support specialized DSP hardware instructions like MAC (Multiply-and-Accumulate) with saturation. To bridge this, compilers provide intrinsics , function-like commands that map directly to assembly instructions.
// Example of a built-in intrinsic for dsPIC (XC16)
// Performs a 16x16 multiply and accumulates to an accumulator
__builtin_mac(a, b, &accumulator, ...);


Circular Buffers
DSP algorithms (like FIR filters) often require sliding windows over data. Circular buffers allow the pointer to wrap around automatically when it reaches the end of the buffer, often supported by hardware modulo addressing.


The DSP Library
Microchip provides a DSP library (often included with the compiler) containing optimized functions for:

Vector operations (add, subtract, dot product)
Filters (FIR, IIR)
Transforms (FFT)

Using these pre-validated libraries is often more efficient than writing raw C implementations.

title: The C Language
text:
Common Pitfalls and Best Practices
C gives you enormous power and freedom, but with that comes the responsibility to avoid subtle bugs. Here are the most common traps that snare even experienced programmers.

1. Integer Promotion and Implicit Conversions
C’s type promotion rules are surprising. In expressions mixing different integer types, smaller types are promoted to larger types.
int16_t a = 30000;
int16_t b = 30000;

// Wrong! Overflow before assignment
int32_t result = a + b;  // a + b happens in 16-bit: -5536
                         // Then promoted to int32_t

// Correct: Promote before arithmetic
int32_t result = (int32_t)a + b;  // First term is int32_t, b is promoted
Rule of thumb: When doing arithmetic that might overflow, explicitly cast the first operand to the desired result type.


2. Operator Precedence Surprises
// Common mistake
if (flags & MASK == ENABLED)  // Wrong! Parsed as: flags & (MASK == ENABLED)

// Correct
if ((flags & MASK) == ENABLED)  // Mask first, then compare
Bitwise operators (&, |, ^) have lower precedence than comparison operators (==, !=). Always use parentheses.

3. Assignment vs. Comparison
if (x = 5)  // Oops! Assignment, not comparison
            // Always true (5 is non-zero)

if (x == 5) // Correct
Defensive programming: Some teams write constants first (Yoda conditions):
if (5 == x)  // If you accidentally type =, compiler error!


4. Uninitialized Variables
int16_t sample;  // Garbage value!
process_sample(sample);  // Undefined behavior

int16_t sample = 0;  // Always initialize
Global and static variables are automatically zero-initialized. Local variables are not.


5. Buffer Overruns
The classic C vulnerability:
char buffer[10];
strcpy(buffer, "This string is way too long");  // Buffer overflow!

// Safe alternatives
strncpy(buffer, source, sizeof(buffer) - 1);
buffer[sizeof(buffer) - 1] = '\0';  // Ensure null termination
Or better yet, use snprintf:
snprintf(buffer, sizeof(buffer), "Value: %d", x);


6. Off-by-One Errors
int array[10];
for(int i = 0; i <= 10; i++) {  // Wrong! Accesses array[10] which doesn't exist
    array[i] = 0;
}

// Correct
for(int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    array[i] = 0;
}
Mnemonic: Use < for counting up to a size, > for counting down to zero.


7. Pointer Arithmetic Gone Wrong
int16_t *ptr = malloc(10 * sizeof(int16_t));
ptr++;  // Now points to second element

free(ptr);  // WRONG! Must free the original pointer
Rule: Never free() a pointer that has been modified. Keep the original pointer.


8. Modifying String Literals
char *str = "Hello";  // String literal in read-only memory
str[0] = 'h';         // Undefined behavior! Might crash

// Correct: Array on stack (modifiable)
char str[] = "Hello";
str[0] = 'h';  // OK


9. Forgetting break in switch Statements
switch(state) {
    case STATE_IDLE:
        init_processing();
        // Oops! Falls through to STATE_ACTIVE
    case STATE_ACTIVE:
        process_data();
        break;
}
Fallthrough is rarely intentional. Always use break unless you explicitly want fallthrough (and comment it!):
case STATE_WARNING:
    flash_led();
    // FALLTHROUGH  (intentional)
case STATE_ERROR:
    halt_system();
    break;


10. Macro Side Effects
#define MAX(a,b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))

int x = 5;
int result = MAX(x++, 10);  // x incremented TWICE if x > 10!
Macros expand textually. If the argument has side effects, they happen multiple times.
Solution: Use inline functions:
static inline int max(int a, int b) {
    return (a > b) ? a : b;
}


11. Undefined Behavior

The Worst Kind of Bug

Some operations have undefined behavior: the C standard places no requirements on what happens. The program might work, crash, or corrupt data silently.

Common sources

Signed integer overflow: INT_MAX + 1 is undefined (use unsigned for modulo arithmetic)
Null pointer dereference: *ptr where ptr == NULL
Accessing freed memory: “use after free”
Array out of bounds: arr[100] when arr has size 50
Uninitialized variables: Reading before writing
Violating strict aliasing: Casting pointer types incorrectly







WarningStupid Optimizer



The optimizer assumes undefined behavior never happens and optimizes accordingly, potentially causing bizarre bugs in release builds that don’t appear in debug builds.

title: The Assembly Language
text:
Assembly language is the closest humans have ever come to speaking directly to a machine. Before we get to the dsPIC specifics, it helps to understand where assembly sits in the history of programming languages — because that context explains why assembly works the way it does and why it still matters.
In the earliest days of computing (1940s–1950s), programmers wrote in machine code — raw binary or hexadecimal opcodes entered by hand, switch by switch. 0x778210 is a MOV instruction. Good luck remembering that. This was first-generation programming. Assembly language arrived as the second-generation language: instead of writing 0x778210, you write MOV W0, W1. The assembler — a program — translates those human-readable mnemonics one-for-one into the binary opcodes the processor actually executes. One mnemonic, one machine instruction. That 1:1 relationship is the defining characteristic of assembly. There is no abstraction, no compilation strategy, no runtime. What you write is what the CPU runs.
Third-generation languages — C, Fortran, Pascal — introduced real abstraction. One line of C might become dozens of assembly instructions. This is both the power and the cost of high-level languages. The C compiler does the translation for you, and it does it well, but you lose direct visibility into what the processor is actually doing. Here is the insight that makes assembly worth studying even today: C is compiled to assembly. Every for loop, every if statement, every function call — the compiler turns all of it into the same register loads, branches, and arithmetic that you will write by hand in this chapter. Learning assembly means learning what C actually does, not just what it says.
The relationship between assembly and processor architecture is tight and interesting. When processor designers shifted from CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computing) to RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computing) architectures in the 1980s and 1990s, assembly language changed with them. CISC processors like x86 accumulated hundreds of instructions over decades — there are x86 instructions for computing BCD arithmetic and string comparisons that no C compiler has touched in thirty years. RISC architectures took the opposite philosophy: a small, uniform set of simple instructions, each completing in one clock cycle. The dsPIC33F is a RISC-influenced architecture. Its instruction set is clean and regular: 16-bit registers, load-store memory model, predictable timing. That predictability is not an accident — it is what makes the dsPIC suitable for real-time DSP, where you need to know exactly how many cycles your filter will take.
In C, you write for(int i = 0; i < N; i++) and the compiler generates the assembly to load, compare, decrement, and branch. In assembly, you manage every step explicitly.
This guide covers assembly language fundamentals with specific focus on the dsPIC33F architecture used in this course. You will learn the instruction set, addressing modes, and DSP-specific features that enable real-time signal processing.
